# Symmetric vs Asymmetric Cryptography

Two families with different guarantees and wildly different costs. **Neither replaces the other** —
every real protocol uses both, and understanding why is the point of labs 03–06 in
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]].

## The two problems symmetric cryptography cannot solve

One shared secret used for both encryption and decryption is fast and simple, and fails twice:

1. **Key distribution.** The recipient must already have the key, and getting it to them over the same
   untrusted channel is the original problem restated.
2. **Key count.** Every *pair* of parties needs its own key, or a third party in the group can read
   traffic that is not theirs. *n* participants need *n(n−1)/2* keys.

Asymmetric cryptography dissolves both: each party publishes one key and keeps one, so *n*
participants need *n* keypairs and the public half can travel over any channel. What it does **not**
give you for free is knowing *whose* public key you hold — that is a trust problem, not a maths
problem, and it is what [[public-key-infrastructure]] exists to answer.

## Why it is slow, and what "slow" means

Asymmetric schemes rest on one-way functions — problems easy in one direction and hard in reverse.
RSA rests on integer factorisation (see [[rsa-and-integer-factorization]]); Diffie–Hellman, DSA,
ElGamal and the elliptic-curve family rest on discrete logarithms. Both involve modular exponentiation
over very large integers, which is orders of magnitude more expensive per byte than a block cipher's
round function.

Lab 04's design is the right way to establish this. Encryption time is measured across **two** varying
factors at once — RSA key length (512, 1024, 2048 bits) against input size (1, 5, 10 MB) — with input
diversity held as a third axis carried over from lab 03. Varying both separates *what actually drives
cost*: key length dominates per-operation cost, input size dominates total cost, and input entropy
turns out to drive neither. A single-variable experiment would have conflated them.

The fixtures for that measurement are generated rather than committed — see
[[generate-fixtures-not-commit]].

## The hybrid construction

The resolution every deployed protocol reaches: **encrypt the data with a symmetric cipher, encrypt
only the symmetric key with the asymmetric one.** One expensive public-key operation on a few hundred
bits, then a fast block cipher on the payload. TLS, PGP, S/MIME and encrypted-messaging protocols are
all this shape.

The alternative to shipping a wrapped key is agreeing one: Diffie–Hellman derives a shared secret
from public exchanges, so nothing secret crosses the wire at all. Lab 06 attempts DH both as a
CrypTool demonstration and practically over OpenSSL between two VMs — and the OpenSSL half is one of
the repository's recorded failures ("did not work", "not resolved"). **TODO:** whether it was later
completed is unrecorded. The DH concept is evidenced from the lab's written answers; the practical
exchange is not evidenced as having succeeded. `confidence: low` on that specific exercise.

DH's own weakness is stated in the same report and is the reason the two labs that follow exist:
unauthenticated key agreement is defeated by a [[man-in-the-middle-attack]], so DH must be signed —
which returns to [[digital-signatures]] and [[public-key-infrastructure]].

## Key-length intuition

Key lengths are not comparable across families. 128-bit symmetric ≈ 3072-bit RSA ≈ 256-bit elliptic
curve, roughly, for equivalent work factor. The lab's own answer puts 2048-bit RSA at "generally
secure for most purposes" with 3072/4096 for stronger requirements — accurate for 2022, and the sort
of claim that needs a date attached, which is why this page carries `valid_from`.
